comments.author: chouky
comments.body:
So basically, you’re buying small positions in the day’s worst-performing 2x ETFs and letting mean reversion do the work.  
That’s a pretty interesting framework, especially with the position caps and staggered entries.  
The fact that those two four-week pauses made such a big difference is probably the most surprising part.  
My only concern would be how many different combinations were tested on the same historical data.  
Once you try enough entry sizes, limits, stops and pause periods, one combination will inevitably look amazing.  
AI makes that search much faster, but it can also make overfitting much easier.  
That doesn’t mean there’s no real edge here—it just makes a clean out-of-sample test essential.  
I’d also check the exact timing of the ranking and limit orders to avoid any same-day look-ahead.  
Ideally, the final rules would be frozen before testing them on data they’ve never seen.  
Have you tried a proper walk-forward test yet?

comments.author: supferrets
comments.body:
The underlying idea might have an edge, but your methodology is fatally flawed. You’re likely inducing same day look ahead bias. The system observes the closing return, selects the two worst performers, looks backward at that day’s low, then credits a limit fill that supposedly happened earlier. This is mechanically impossible.

The 03-22 history is synthetic, if the ETFs or underlying stocks were selected and then projected backward, you now have hindsight and survivorship bias.

You say you tested many entry sizes, order limits, position counts, pauses and other conditions, then asked the AI to give you the best final result. Now you have winner-selection bias. The oddly specific calendar pauses and “March calls” are fitted historical accidents.

A 20% cap per stock means over $10M in one ETF. 2x ETFs are too thin to absorb that capital without slippage and serious market impact.

I see 4,158 share purchases but only 3,782 exits. Either 376 entry lots remain open or the counting needs an explanation.

By the standards I hard code into my governance contracts, you would fail on data lineage, timestamp integrity, selection accounting and executable fill gates before ever even considering performance.
